title: Human verdicts on the 2026-10-09 random-sample audit review queue
verdict_rule: Every tier-1 and tier-2 row in the rows file gets exactly one verdict here. 'false_positive' = the domain belongs to an organisation, product or person using it for their OWN mail, so blocking it blocks real correspondence. 'disposable' = the list is right about it. 'inconclusive' = the live evidence does not settle it either way (parked, for sale, default hosting page, expired domain now serving unrelated content, or a title that only repeats the domain name). Confidence 'high' requires TWO independent legs: a live web root that names a distinct real-world organisation/product/person matching the domain, AND mail hosting that is paid per mailbox or an enterprise gateway. One leg alone, or an organisation that cannot be placed from the page itself, is 'medium'. The headline rate counts 'high' only; 'high + medium' is reported as the upper band.
known_rule_gaps: The triage regex DISPOSABLE_TITLE does not match the phrase 'Temporary Email' (it requires 'temporary mail' / 'tempmail'), so tetses.my.id reached tier 2 instead of tier 3. Caught in review, not by the rule. A miss in this direction only costs review time; it cannot create a false positive.

'business-mx:google' fires on Google Workspace, which a throwaway-mail farm CAN buy. Seven domains in the single-source sample share the exact fingerprint 'MX 1 smtp.google.com + google-site-verification + HTTP 404' and are almost certainly one farm's tenants. The rule promoted them to review and review cleared them, which is the intended behaviour, but Workspace MX on its own is not evidence of a real organisation.
